imo-1978-01.title: Split $1000=8\cdot125$
imo-1978-01.body:
The condition is $1000\mid 1978^n-1978^m=1978^m\,(1978^{n-m}-1)$.

**The factor $8$.** $1978^{n-m}-1$ is odd, so $8\mid1978^m=2^m\cdot989^m$, i.e. $m\ge3$.

**The factor $125$.** $\gcd(1978,125)=1$, so we need $125\mid1978^{d}-1$ with $d=n-m\ge1$, i.e. $d$ is a multiple of the order of $1978$ modulo $125$. This order divides $\varphi(125)=100$. Modulo $5$, $1978\equiv3$, whose order is $4$; so the order mod $125$ is a multiple of $4$ dividing $100$: $4$, $20$ or $100$. Now $1978\equiv-22\pmod{125}$ and
$$(-22)^2=484\equiv-16,\qquad(-22)^4\equiv256\equiv6,\qquad(-22)^{20}\equiv6^5=7776\equiv26\pmod{125}.$$
Neither is $1$, so the order is $100$ and $100\mid n-m$.

**Minimum.** $m+n=2m+(n-m)\ge2\cdot3+100=106$, with equality for $m=3$, $n=103$, which indeed works.

**Answer: $m=3$, $n=103$** (so $m+n=106$).

imo-1978-02.title: Vectors, then a lemma on quadratic forms for the converse
imo-1978-02.body:
Let $O$ be the centre (as the origin) and $R$ the radius; write $\mathbf p=\vec{OP}$, so $|\mathbf p|<R$.

**$Q$ lies on the sphere.** Let $\mathbf u=\vec{PU}$, $\mathbf v=\vec{PV}$, $\mathbf w=\vec{PW}$, mutually perpendicular. Then $\vec{OQ}=\mathbf p+\mathbf u+\mathbf v+\mathbf w$ (the box is a rectangular one). From $|\mathbf p+\mathbf u|^2=R^2$:
$$|\mathbf p|^2+2\,\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf u+|\mathbf u|^2=R^2,$$
and similarly for $\mathbf v,\mathbf w$. Adding,
$$3|\mathbf p|^2+2\,\mathbf p\cdot(\mathbf u+\mathbf v+\mathbf w)+|\mathbf u|^2+|\mathbf v|^2+|\mathbf w|^2=3R^2 .$$
By perpendicularity $|\mathbf p+\mathbf u+\mathbf v+\mathbf w|^2=|\mathbf p|^2+2\,\mathbf p\cdot(\mathbf u+\mathbf v+\mathbf w)+|\mathbf u|^2+|\mathbf v|^2+|\mathbf w|^2$, so
$$OQ^2=3R^2-2\,OP^2 .$$

**Every point of this sphere occurs.** Let $|\mathbf q|^2=3R^2-2|\mathbf p|^2$ and $\mathbf d=\mathbf q-\mathbf p$. For an orthonormal basis $\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2,\mathbf e_3$ put $U_i=\mathbf p+(\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf e_i)\mathbf e_i$; then $\mathbf p+\sum_i(\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf e_i)\mathbf e_i=\mathbf q$. We need all $|U_i|=R$, i.e.
$$\mathbf e_i^{\mathsf T}S\,\mathbf e_i=c\quad(i=1,2,3),\qquad S=\mathbf p\mathbf d^{\mathsf T}+\mathbf d\mathbf p^{\mathsf T}+\mathbf d\mathbf d^{\mathsf T},\ c=R^2-|\mathbf p|^2,$$
since $|U_i|^2-|\mathbf p|^2=2(\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf e_i)(\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf e_i)+(\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf e_i)^2$. Here $\operatorname{tr}S=2\,\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf d+|\mathbf d|^2=|\mathbf q|^2-|\mathbf p|^2=3c$.

*Lemma: a symmetric $3\times3$ matrix $T$ with trace $0$ has an orthonormal basis with all $\mathbf e_i^{\mathsf T}T\mathbf e_i=0$.* Apply it to $T=S-cI$. Proof: let $\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\lambda_3$ be the eigenvalues (sum $0$, so $\lambda_1\le0\le\lambda_3$) with orthonormal eigenvectors $\mathbf f_1,\mathbf f_3$. If $\lambda_1=\lambda_3$, then $T=0$. Otherwise $\mathbf e_1=\frac{\sqrt{\lambda_3}\,\mathbf f_1+\sqrt{-\lambda_1}\,\mathbf f_3}{\sqrt{\lambda_3-\lambda_1}}$ is a unit vector with $\mathbf e_1^{\mathsf T}T\mathbf e_1=\frac{\lambda_3\lambda_1-\lambda_1\lambda_3}{\lambda_3-\lambda_1}=0$. On the plane $\mathbf e_1^\perp$ the form has trace $\operatorname{tr}T-0=0$, so for an orthonormal basis $\mathbf g(\varphi),\mathbf h(\varphi)$ of that plane rotated by angle $\varphi$, the value $\mathbf g(\varphi)^{\mathsf T}T\mathbf g(\varphi)=-\mathbf h(\varphi)^{\mathsf T}T\mathbf h(\varphi)$; as $\mathbf g(\frac\pi2)=\mathbf h(0)$, this continuous function changes sign on $[0,\frac\pi2]$ and vanishes at some $\varphi$. Take $\mathbf e_2=\mathbf g(\varphi)$, $\mathbf e_3=\mathbf h(\varphi)$.

With this basis each $U_i$ is on the sphere; $t_i=\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf e_i\ne0$ since $P$ itself is not on the sphere. The three rays from $P$ in the directions $t_i\mathbf e_i$ are mutually perpendicular, each meets the sphere exactly once (as $P$ is inside), namely at $U_i$, and the opposite vertex of the box is $\mathbf p+\sum t_i\mathbf e_i=\mathbf q$.

**Answer: the locus is the whole sphere centred at $O$ with radius $\sqrt{3R^2-2\,OP^2}$.** ∎

imo-1978-03.title: The sequences are Beatty sequences for $\varphi$
imo-1978-03.body:
Let $\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$, so $\varphi^2=\varphi+1$ and $\frac1\varphi+\frac1{\varphi^2}=1$.

**Uniqueness.** The conditions determine $f$ and $g$. Indeed, suppose we already know which of $1,\ldots,N$ are $f$-values and which are $g$-values, and let $j$ be the number of $g$-values $\le N$. The next number $N+1$ is a $g$-value iff $N+1=g(j+1)=f(f(j+1))+1$, i.e. iff $f(f(j+1))=N$; since $f(j+1)\le f(f(j+1))$, this can be decided from the known $f$-values $\le N$. Otherwise $N+1$ is an $f$-value. So by induction there is at most one pair $(f,g)$.

**Existence: $f(n)=\lfloor n\varphi\rfloor$, $g(n)=\lfloor n\varphi^2\rfloor=\lfloor n\varphi\rfloor+n$.**
* *They partition the positive integers (Beatty).* Both are strictly increasing since $\varphi,\varphi^2>1$. The number of $n$ with $\lfloor n\varphi\rfloor\le N$ is the number with $n\varphi<N+1$, i.e. $\lfloor\frac{N+1}{\varphi}\rfloor$ (no equality, $\varphi$ irrational); similarly for $\varphi^2$. As $\frac{N+1}\varphi+\frac{N+1}{\varphi^2}=N+1$ with both terms non-integers, their floors add up to $N$. So exactly $N$ terms of the two sequences together are $\le N$ for every $N$, hence each positive integer appears exactly once.
* *The relation.* Let $m=\lfloor n\varphi\rfloor=n\varphi-\varepsilon$ with $0<\varepsilon<1$. Then
$$m\varphi=n\varphi^2-\varepsilon\varphi=n\varphi+n-\varepsilon\varphi=m+n-\varepsilon(\varphi-1)=m+n-\frac{\varepsilon}{\varphi},$$
and $0<\frac\varepsilon\varphi<1$, so $f(f(n))=\lfloor m\varphi\rfloor=m+n-1$ and $f(f(n))+1=\lfloor n\varphi\rfloor+n=g(n)$. ✓

**Computation.** $f(240)=\lfloor120(1+\sqrt5)\rfloor=120+\lfloor\sqrt{72000}\rfloor=120+268=388$, because $268^2=71824\le72000<72361=269^2$.

**Answer: $f(240)=388$.**

imo-1978-04.title: Compute both distances from $A$ along the axis
imo-1978-04.body:
Let $\Gamma$ (centre $O$, radius $R$) be the circumcircle, $\omega$ (centre $K$, radius $\rho$) the given circle, $I$ the incentre, and $\alpha=\frac12\angle BAC$. The figure is symmetric about the axis $\ell$ through $A$ and the midpoint of $BC$, which contains $O$; let $T$ be the second intersection of $\ell$ with $\Gamma$, so $AT=2R$ is a diameter.

**Where $\omega$ sits.** $K$ is equidistant from lines $AB,AC$ and inside the angle, so $K\in\ell$ and $AK=\frac{\rho}{\sin\alpha}$. The tangency point of $\omega$ and $\Gamma$ lies on the line of centres $OK=\ell$, so it is $A$ or $T$. It is not $A$: otherwise $A\in\omega$ would lie on the tangent line $AB$ of $\omega$, forcing $A=P$, and likewise $A=Q$, but a circle has only one tangent line at a point. So $\omega$ touches $\Gamma$ at $T$, and since $K$ lies on segment $AT$, $AK+KT=AT$:
$$\frac{\rho}{\sin\alpha}+\rho=2R\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\rho=\frac{2R\sin\alpha}{1+\sin\alpha}.$$

**The midpoint $M$ of $PQ$.** By symmetry $M\in\ell$ and $PQ\perp\ell$. In right triangle $APK$ (right angle at $P$), $AP=AK\cos\alpha$, and $AM=AP\cos\alpha$, so
$$AM=\frac{\rho\cos^2\alpha}{\sin\alpha}=\frac{2R\cos^2\alpha}{1+\sin\alpha}=2R(1-\sin\alpha).$$

**The incentre.** $I\in\ell$ lies between $A$ and $T$ (inside the triangle; $T$ is beyond $BC$). We have $TB=TI$: indeed $\angle TBI=\angle TBC+\angle CBI=\angle TAC+\frac B2=\alpha+\frac B2$ (inscribed angles on arc $TC$), and $\angle TIB$ is an exterior angle of triangle $ABI$, equal to $\angle BAI+\angle ABI=\alpha+\frac B2$. In the right triangle $ABT$ ($AT$ a diameter), $TB=AT\sin\angle BAT=2R\sin\alpha$. Hence
$$AI=AT-TI=2R-2R\sin\alpha=AM .$$

Both $M$ and $I$ lie on the ray from $A$ along $\ell$ at the same distance from $A$, so $M=I$. ∎

imo-1978-05.title: Rearrangement
imo-1978-05.body:
Fix $n$ and let $b_1<b_2<\cdots<b_n$ be the numbers $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ in increasing order. Since they are distinct positive integers, $b_k\ge k$ for each $k$ (by induction: $b_1\ge1$ and $b_{k+1}\ge b_k+1$).

**Sorting lowers the sum.** If $i<j$ but $a_i>a_j$, swapping $a_i$ and $a_j$ changes $\sum\frac{a_k}{k^2}$ by
$$\Big(\frac{a_j}{i^2}+\frac{a_i}{j^2}\Big)-\Big(\frac{a_i}{i^2}+\frac{a_j}{j^2}\Big)=-(a_i-a_j)\Big(\frac1{i^2}-\frac1{j^2}\Big)<0 .$$
Repeating such swaps (each reduces the number of inversions) ends at the sorted order $b_1,\ldots,b_n$, so
$$\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{a_k}{k^2}\ge\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{b_k}{k^2}\ge\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{k}{k^2}=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1k. \qquad ∎$$

imo-1978-05.title: Cauchy–Schwarz
imo-1978-05.body:
With $b_k$ as above, $\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1{a_k}=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1{b_k}\le\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1k=:H$. By Cauchy–Schwarz,
$$H^2=\Big(\sum_{k=1}^n\sqrt{\frac{a_k}{k^2}}\cdot\sqrt{\frac1{a_k}}\Big)^2\le\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{a_k}{k^2}\cdot\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1{a_k}\le\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{a_k}{k^2}\cdot H .$$
Dividing by $H>0$ gives $\sum\frac{a_k}{k^2}\ge H$. ∎

imo-1978-06.title: Repeated pigeonhole on differences
imo-1978-06.body:
Suppose no member has this property: no number of a country is the sum of two (possibly equal) numbers of the same country.

**Basic observation.** If $x>y$ are both in country $C$, then $x-y\notin C$: otherwise $x=y+(x-y)$ with $y,x-y\in C$ (if $y=x-y$, then $x$ is twice a number of $C$).

We build sets $B_1\supseteq B_2\supseteq\cdots$ of numbers and distinct countries $C_1,C_2,\ldots$ such that

> $(\star_k)$ for all $x>y$ in $B_k$, the difference $x-y$ belongs to none of $C_1,\ldots,C_k$.

**Start.** Some country $C_1$ has at least $\lceil1978/6\rceil=330$ members; let $B_1=C_1$. By the observation, $(\star_1)$ holds.

**Step $k\to k+1$** ($k\le5$). Let $m_k=|B_k|$ and let $b$ be the smallest element of $B_k$. The $m_k-1$ numbers $x-b$ ($x\in B_k$, $x>b$) are distinct, lie in $\{1,\ldots,1977\}$, and by $(\star_k)$ belong to the remaining $6-k$ countries. So some country $C_{k+1}$ contains at least $\big\lceil\frac{m_k-1}{6-k}\big\rceil$ of them; let $B_{k+1}$ be the set of those $x$ with $x-b\in C_{k+1}$. Then $(\star_{k+1})$ holds: for $x>y$ in $B_{k+1}$, the difference $x-y$ is not in $C_1,\ldots,C_k$ by $(\star_k)$ (as $B_{k+1}\subseteq B_k$), and not in $C_{k+1}$ by the basic observation, since $x-y=(x-b)-(y-b)$ is a difference of two elements of $C_{k+1}$.

**Counting.**
$$m_1\ge330,\quad m_2\ge\Big\lceil\tfrac{329}{5}\Big\rceil=66,\quad m_3\ge\Big\lceil\tfrac{65}{4}\Big\rceil=17,\quad m_4\ge\Big\lceil\tfrac{16}{3}\Big\rceil=6,\quad m_5\ge\Big\lceil\tfrac{5}{2}\Big\rceil=3,\quad m_6\ge\Big\lceil\tfrac21\Big\rceil=2 .$$

**Contradiction.** $B_6$ has two elements $x>y$; their difference is a number in $\{1,\ldots,1977\}$, so it belongs to some member, i.e. to one of the six countries — but by $(\star_6)$ it is in none of $C_1,\ldots,C_6$. Hence the assumption was false. ∎
